description: Applies the FSharp.Refactor analyzers' quick fixes to F# code from the command line. Point it at a project, a script, a solution, a directory or a glob; --dry-run reports without editing. The tool clarifies the (agent-generated or old) code's intent, reduces non-alphanumeric noise, and uses built-in .NET libraries more efficiently.
releaseNotes:
0.8.34: Silent sweep rewrites closed, each shown by a failing test before its guard went in - and every guard built the same way round: the fix by default, a note only where the analysis positively finds the edge, never for want of a proof. FR0172 names a tail read beside the second element `h :: (s :: _ as t)`: `h :: s :: t` bound the rest after the second, one short of `.Tail`, and typechecked; and it declines an arm whose body starts on the `->` line and continues below, a line right under a lengthening edit indented past it, a line aligned exactly to a token a shortening edit moves, or a single-line arm with a line below anchored to text after it, since the moved text would push those lines offside (FS0058) or read them as arguments, with no compile error to stop it. FR0168 keeps the try where the Parse argument is a shape that throws on its own - an index (`args.[1]`), a cut or a parse of its own (`s.Substring 5`, `Convert.ToInt32 x`), a numeric conversion (`int x`, `Checked.int x`), a `.Value`/`.Head` read anywhere in the chain (`o.Value.Trim()`) of an option, a Nullable, a Lazy or a list - never a KeyValuePair's or a record's - or a downcast (`o :?> string`), or a partial function of FSharp.Core (`List.head`, `Option.get`, `Map.find`, `Map.pick`) - since the catch answered that exception with the fallback too; a getter, a user call, a `Trim` is taken as a read and the fix stands; `TimeSpan` joins the types whose Parse overflows. FR0170 keeps the loop only on what it sees write the dictionary before a read: the receiver handed on, reassigned or rebound, a store through a value of this file bound to it - by name, a tuple pattern or a record field - or through a setter of this file (a store runs the setter, a read the getter), a function, member, getter, active pattern or forced `seq`/`async`/`lazy` value defined in this file whose body touches a dictionary (a `let mutable` hook by every body assigned to it in this file; an auto-property is a dictionary, a read through `ContainsKey` or `Count` is no touch), and in a `seq { }` or `task { }` each `yield`, `let!` and `do!` (an else-less `if` or a loop with a value is an implicit yield, a unit statement is not) - a getter counted where it is read, argument or not, every loop nested around a read counted whole, a read inside a local function keeping the loop, and a receiver segment whose getter of this file builds a dictionary, itself or through a helper of this file, too. A `log k`, an interface call, a delegate, an event, a helper defined in another file, LINQ, a field store, a write to another dictionary: the fix, since nothing visible says otherwise; the accepted residual is user code behind such a call writing the very dictionary the loop walks. FR0060's eager-filter probe takes a dotted read as total unless a segment is a member known to throw - `.Value` of an option, a Nullable or a Lazy, `.Head`/`.Tail` of a list, an indexer, `.Force()`, a Memory's `.Span` - so `s.Length` and a user getter fire as FSharpLint's own hint does. FR0166's length guard proves the cut for an immutable value (never a byref) and for a `let mutable` not written between the guard and the cut - a local one by a `<-` or a `&` there, so the `while not (isNull line)` reader loop stays exact; a module or class one also by a call there whose body, defined in this file, assigns it - itself, through the calls it makes, or by a `&` to it, whatever module path the receiver reaches it by, and never another mutable of that name in another scope; the rest of an `if` condition after the guard and a loop between count as between - qualified by modules or read through immutable fields, get-only `member val`s and BCL getters. FR0167 writes `FSharp.Core.Operators.nonNull` and FR0173 `FSharp.Core.Operators.max 0 n`, which no `nonNull`, `max` or module named `Operators` of the project's own can take. FR0164's RemoveAll fix gives way to the snapshot for a condition reading a `let mutable` or a Span, or a loop holding a comment, and its editor offers pass the comment guard. The analyzers no longer hold a thread-pool thread while a deep-stack worker runs a rule. Each queued analyzer blocked one, and on a large project - the dogfood step over the analyzers project itself - every pool thread ended up waiting on a worker while the worker waited on the thread pool for the FCS parse of the default hints behind a lazy: a deadlock that never finished. The analyzer now awaits its worker instead.

 0.8.33: The analyzers no longer walk the whole file once per candidate. About thirty rules asked which expressions sit inside a range by testing every expression of the file for each hit, a cost that grew with the square of the file: on an 18k-line file SeqEnumeratedTwice (FR0169) took 5.7 s, FailwithContext (FR0092) 6.6 s, SwallowedException (FR0055) 4.3 s and Accumulation (FR0050/FR0107) 3.5 s of their own work; they now take 9 to 43 ms, UseBinding and AccumulatorLoop (FR0156) about 0.7 s. The shared pieces: `AstIndex.exprsWithin`/`patsWithin`, a range query over a per-file start order that returns exactly the nodes a walk finds, in its order; `AstIndex.mentionsOf`, where each name is read; per-file tables behind the helpers FR0107, the Option/Result wrappers and FR0012 share; and `OptionModule.symbolUseAt`, a per-file memo of FCS's `GetSymbolUseAtLocation` that every typed lookup of the rules goes through. Every message and fix is unchanged - byte-identical on synthetic 4.5k- and 18k-line files, identical dry-run reports on five real projects - and a dry-run sweep of the analyzers project went from 384 s to 229 s, of the tool project from 89 s to 35 s. The analyzers' own code takes its performance notes: single-character `StartsWith`/`EndsWith` use the char overload, two recursive `seq { yield! }` walks became one, a list's length is read once outside its loop. The api pass no longer takes a build-order-only `ProjectReference` (`ReferenceOutputAssembly` false) for a consumer, unless the project also references the built dll directly: every pass over this repository's own Ionide twin loaded the Analyzers project and both test projects behind it only to report each "cannot be read". The end-to-end tests that build a synthetic solution carry `Category=Slow`, so `dotnet test --filter "Category!=Slow"` leaves them out.

 0.8.32: FR0173 takes a mapper spanning lines only as a lambda whose body starts on a line of its own. A `match` or a first statement after the arrow moves with that line: `(fun i -> match i with` over arms aligned to the `match` fell offside (FS0058) when the count's `max 0` made the line longer, and a second statement aligned to a first one became its argument when the line got shorter - `tap i` over `i` read as `tap i i`, a changed result with no compile error to stop it.

 0.8.31: FR0035 converts a list whose element can carry a float to a `Set` only when every element is a written-out non-NaN constant, since the Set finds a NaN `List.contains` never did. FR0167's String twins go through `nonNull` on FSharp.Core 9+, which throws on a null string as the copy did, so a sweep applies them. FR0041 sweeps `Array.contains v arr` on `int[]`/`int64[]` to `Enumerable.Contains(arr, v)`, exact on those types; the aggregations stay notes. FR0174 sweeps a nullable column of an exact type compared by `=`/`<`/`<=`/`>`/`>=` with a non-null value outside any `not`, where SQL and .NET both drop the NULL row. FR0071 no longer hoists a division by a signed integral `-1` (`MinValue / -1` overflows) or anything in a file under `open Checked`.

 0.8.30: FR0174 (performance, fix), CR0178's twin: in C#-style LINQ over `open System.Linq`, a query copied before `Where`/`Select` loads every row - `db.Orders.ToList().Where(fun o -> o.Total > 0).Select(fun o -> o.Id)` becomes `db.Orders.Where(fun o -> o.Total > 0).Select(fun o -> o.Id).ToList()`, for value-column comparisons and projections only, and by a sweep only where the chain's new List type binds as the IEnumerable did; the pipeline shape is behind the default-off `pipelines` knob. A review of the whole code closed some eighty defects, each reproduced by a failing test: non-UTF-8 files were rewritten with U+FFFD (now read in the system code page and put back byte for byte), the verification build stopped at its first failure without building consumers, a timeout left earlier passes' fixes unverified, and silent rewrites in FR0166, FR0010, FR0035, FR0021, FR0006, FR0170, FR0060, FR0075, FR0004, FR0005, FR0119, FR0049, FR0118, FR0160, FR0071, FR0026, FR0053, FR0023, FR0029, FR0034 and FR0157 (record-field rewrites now editor-only) got guards; FR0049 reads `winner = work && work.IsCompleted && work.Result` as a read; a C# consumer's escalated analyzer error (CA/IDE) counts as a code error.

 0.8.29: FR0173 (performance, fix): a range built only to be mapped over allocates a second collection the size of the result - `[| 0 .. dimension - 1 |] |> Array.map f` is `Array.init dimension f`. Measured (.NET 10, a million elements): 7.0 ms and 8,000,099 B become 3.3 ms and 4,000,044 B, twice as fast on half the allocation. A sweep applies it only where the count is provably non-negative (a length, a count, a literal), since the empty range maps to an empty result where init raises ArgumentException; the editor offers it either way. FR0172 (idiom, fix): a match arm that binds a whole list only to read `itms.[0]` (or `itms[0]`, `itms.Head`, `List.head itms`), `itms.[1]` or `itms.Tail` is a cons pattern - `| itms -> g itms.[0]` becomes `| itmsHead :: _ -> g itmsHead`, the tail named only where the arm reads it. Exact where an earlier unguarded `[]` arm (and `[_]` for a second element) already keeps the short lists out of the arm, so the match stays as complete as it was and the compiler's exhaustiveness check stands in for the ArgumentException a list index raises; any other use of the name, an index above 1, a rebinding inside the arm, or an array (`[||]`) or an earlier bare catch-all (which covers every array and string too) stands the rule down. Parse-only, the `[]` arm settling the type. Measured: no run-time difference between the shapes - `xs.[0]` walks no cells - so the rule is the idiom, not speed. FR0156 takes the `let mutable` list beside the ResizeArray: `let mutable xs = []` fed by `xs <- xs @ [ e ]` or `List.append xs [ e ]` inside its loops and only read after becomes the list expression with each element as its yield (measured at 1000 elements: 250x faster on 0.3% of the allocation - every append copied the list), and `xs <- e :: xs` read through `List.rev` alone does too, the reverse becoming the bare name (1.5x on half); an assignment after the loops, a read inside them, a list fed at both ends or a project's own `@` stands it down. FR0050 leaves that combine alone (a fold would keep the copy), and FR0051's note names the list expression first. PerfClaims gains the cases FR0168, FR0170 and FR0171 had not got; FR0171's runs long enough to tier up, since a byte string literal is `InitializeArray` from RVA data, a helper call at tier 0 and a copy at tier 1. FR0071 now leaves an array literal inside the loop where it still hoists a list: a list is immutable, so n allocations become one and nothing can tell, but an array literal is a fresh mutable buffer per iteration and a hoisted one is shared by every pass. FR0015 per-call hoist knob: { "FR0015": { "perCall": false } } keeps the loop hoists and leaves a Regex in a plain function body where it is written; on by default, since a function is far likelier to be called many times than a module is to be initialised with its hoisted binding never read.
